newsitem.title: UK: Sterling set to keep British exporters on the rack.
newsitem.headline: Sterling set to keep British exporters on the rack.

text.p: British exporters and overseas earners are braced for a tough year in 1997 amid growing worries that sterling's rapid rise is unlikely to be significantly reversed in coming months, strategists said on Thursday.

The pound's relentless surge has already prompted many British companies to voice fears that the strength of sterling could damage foreign earnings further and could endanger the fledgling recovery of Britain's manufacturers.

These fears have inevitably filtered through to the market, culminating in a rash of profit downgrades for big foreign earners like British Steel and RTZ Corp -- and with the prospect of more to come in the near future.
"We are looking for the market to take a hit of about two percent (of profitability) as a result of sterling," said Philip Isherwood, strategist at Kleinwort Benson.

It is not just those companies that export abroad that are being hurt as sterling's advance makes their goods more expensive to foreign buyers. A strong pound also depresses the value of British companies' overseas earnings once they are translated back into sterling.
Analysts estimate that around 15 percent of goods produced in Britain by the top 100 quoted companies go abroad, while nearly 50 percent of their profits are derived from their businesses overseas.
"Looking at the market as a whole you can take around two percent off next year's growth on the strength we are seeing the pound," said Steve Wright, an equity strategist at BZW.
However, he pointed out that analysts' sales growth estimates do not reflect much of a bounce in turnover despite generally strong GDP growth forecasts.
Building materials company BPB Industries said on Thursday that it would continue to be hit by a strengthening sterling in the current financial year.
"We have been hit by three million sterling in the first six months. It could go up to 10 to 15 million sterling for the full year," BPB's managing director Jean-Pierre Cuny told Reuters.
Redland, which derives 40 percent of its sales from Germany, also revealed that the strength of the pound was hitting foreign earnings.
Gordon Campbell, chief executive of chemicals company Courtaulds Plc said recently: "If the strength of sterling to the dollar continues then it is going to make margins tougher."
Courtaulds has a significant British manufacturing base yet only 14 percent of its sales go into the home market.
British Steel has also expressed concern at the strengthening of the pound and its impact on prices and the competitiveness of its customers in their export markets.
Sterling has risen 12 percent on its trade weighted index since the beginning of the year and is trading at its strongest level against the German mark since February 1994.

Currency analysts also see little to dent enthusiasm for the pound in coming months given the prospect of further British interest rate rises and the view that sterling provides a safe-haven from potential turbulence in European currencies in the run-up to European Monetary Union.
